passages.t: A measuring line, and a wall of fire
passages.happening: Zechariah looks up and sees a man with a measuring line in his hand (verse 1). He is going to measure Jerusalem, its width and length (verse 2). Then another angel comes and sends word to the young man: Jerusalem will be a city without walls, because of the great number of people and animals in it (verses 3-4). ‘For I will be a wall of fire around it, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory within it’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This is the third night vision. A measuring line was used to lay out a building or a city, and the young man wants to plan Jerusalem's walls. In 520 BC the city was thinly settled and its walls were broken; it would be decades before Nehemiah rebuilt them.

The angel's message overturns the plan. The city God intends will be too full for walls. Its protection will be God himself, a wall of fire, and its glory will be his presence within. The picture recalls the pillar of fire that led and guarded Israel in the wilderness, and the glory that filled the tabernacle.
passages.later: In the wilderness the LORD went before Israel ‘in a pillar of fire to give them light’ (Exodus 13:21). Ezekiel saw the glory return to the temple (Ezekiel 43:2-5).
passages.asks: The young man wanted to measure walls, and God promised to be the wall. Ask what walls you are trying to build for your own safety. And ask what it would mean to trust God to be your protection.

passages.t: Come home: God will dwell among you
passages.happening:
The exiles still in the north, in Babylon, are called to flee and come home (verses 6-7). Whoever touches God's people touches the apple of his eye, and the nations that plundered them will be plundered by their own servants (verses 8-9).

‘Shout for joy and be glad, O Daughter of Zion, for I am coming to dwell among you,’ declares the LORD (verse 10). ‘On that day many nations will join themselves to the LORD, and they will become My people’ (verse 11). The LORD will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land and will again choose Jerusalem (verse 12). ‘Be silent before the LORD, all people, for He has roused Himself from His holy dwelling’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Many Judeans had stayed in Babylon after Cyrus's decree. The call is to leave and come home before judgment falls on Babylon. The apple of the eye is the pupil, the most protected part of the body: to touch God's people is to touch what he guards most closely.

The most striking line is verse 11. Many nations will join themselves to the LORD and become his people, the covenant words once used of Israel alone.

The phrase holy land appears here for the first time in the Bible. And the last verse calls everyone to silence, because God has stirred himself to act.
passages.later: Isaiah called the exiles out of Babylon: ‘Depart, depart, go out from there’ (Isaiah 52:11). A psalm prays to be kept ‘as the apple of Your eye’ (Psalm 17:8).
passages.hard:
Who is speaking when the text speaks of one whom the LORD of Hosts has sent?

Verses 8 to 11 are hard to follow, because the speaker seems to be both the LORD and someone the LORD has sent. There are three main readings. Many scholars take the speaker as Zechariah himself: the prophet quotes God's words, then adds that when these things happen the people will know God sent him, a claim he makes again in 4:9 and 6:15. Others take the speaker as the angel of the LORD, who throughout the visions speaks for God and yet is distinguished from him. Many Christian interpreters, noticing that the one sent speaks as God and promises to dwell among the people, have read the passage as a hint of the Son sent by the Father. The grammar allows more than one reading, and these notes leave them open.
passages.asks: God says that many nations will join themselves to him and become his people. Ask who you have assumed could never belong to God. And ask what it means to you that God guards his people like the apple of his eye.
